# Hunch — one page, complete

Hunch is a small language for reinforcement-learning environments and games.
You write the rules of a world, say what is rewarded, and leave a `hunch(...)`
blank wherever a decision is made. A world is one file. `hunch train` fills
the blanks and reports what it found: what each agent collects, whether
anything better exists, and what the policy does.

    ./bin/hunch test  world.hunch      # compile, show what each agent sees, check the asserts
    ./bin/hunch train world.hunch      # fill the blanks; saves world.hpol beside the world
    ./bin/hunch run   world.hunch      # one episode, step by step
    ./bin/hunch why   world.hunch      # what every other action would have been worth
    ./bin/hunch play  world.hunch      # take an agent's seat yourself

---

## File shape

```
world Name                    // optional label: one word, no spaces
record Slot { key: int; }     // a named group of fields, before 'state' 
horizon 50                    // optional: max steps per episode (default 100)
param rate = 0.1;             // compile-time constant, overridable from the CLI

state {
  slots: Slot[4];             // an array of records
  hero: Player;               // one record
}
                              //   (omit it when the world remembers nothing)
init  { ... }                 // optional: runs once at the start of an episode
step  { ... }                 // required: runs once per tick
fn name(a, b) { ... }         // optional helpers; no recursion
```

Comments are `//` to end of line. Statements end with `;`.

## Types

`int` and `float` both mean a double at runtime. Arrays are fixed size:

    state {
      x: int = 0;
      cash: float = 0.0;
      grid: int[49];            // zero-initialised
    }

`grid = [1,1,1, 1,0,1];` in `init` fills an array from literals.

A board reads better as rows. `wide N` after a state array's size says how to
print it, and changes nothing else about it:

    board: int[9] wide 3;       // three rows of three, the first row on top
    board: int[42] wide 7 up;   // rows of seven, the first row at the bottom (pieces fall)

`hunch play` and `hunch run` then show it as a grid, with `.` for a zero.

## Statements

    let v = expr;               // also: let v: float = expr;
    v = expr;
    arr[i] = expr;
    if cond { ... } else if cond { ... } else { ... }
    while cond { ... }
    for i in 0..N { ... }       // i runs 0 .. N-1
    return expr;                // inside fn only
    reward(expr);               // single-agent world
    reward(name, expr);         // multi-agent world, by hunch name
    done();                     // end the episode now; the rest of the step does not run
    assert cond;                // stop the run if a rule is violated

## Local arrays

`let` can declare a fixed-size array local to the step or function, which is
how an observation gets built in a loop instead of written out:

```hunch
step {
  let obs: float[8];
  for i in 0..8 { obs[i] = data[i] / 10.0; }
  let a = hunch agent(obs, 4);
}
```

## What lasts

Only `state` lasts from one step to the next. Every `let`, array or not, starts
each step at zero and is gone at the end of its block. To remember something,
declare it in `state`. `let c = c + 1;` is an error: the `c` on the right does
not exist yet.

## Records

A record names a group of fields, and the compiler lays it out flat, so the
whole world is still one snapshot:

```hunch
record Slot {
  key: int;
  last: int;
  freq: int;
}

state {
  slots: Slot[4];
}

step {
  slots[i].key = want;
  let age = step_count() - slots[i].last;
}
```

`slots[0].freq` reads a field; `slots[0]` on its own is an error, and so is
using a record as a value. Records hold `int`, `float`, `bool` or `num`, start
zeroed, and cannot be nested.

## Params

A `param` is a number fixed when the world is compiled, so an experiment can
sweep it without editing the file:

```sh
./bin/hunch train worlds/cache.hunch --param switch_at=45
```

Anything not overridden keeps its declared value. Overrides are part of the
bytecode cache key, so two variants never collide.

## Checking a world

`./bin/hunch test worlds/x.hunch` runs a few episodes with an untrained
policy and reports whether the rules held.

`assert cond;` stops the run with the line and column when the condition is
false. Use it to make a world prove its own rules before training on it:

```hunch
init {
  assert SIZE > 0;
}

step {
  assert score >= 0;
}
```

A broken rule then fails in a second, rather than producing a training curve
that looks plausible and means nothing.

## Expressions

`+ - * / %`, comparisons `== != < <= > >=`, `&& || !`, unary `-`, indexing
`arr[i]` (out-of-range indices are clamped), parentheses.

Built-ins: `rand()` in [0,1), `randint(lo, hi)` inclusive, `abs(x)`, `min(a,b)`,
`max(a,b)`, `clamp(x,lo,hi)`, `floor(x)`, `sqrt(x)`, `exp(x)`, `step_count()`.

Division by zero yields 0. Recursion is rejected at compile time.
`step_count()` is 1 in the first step.

Prefer `randint` for chance. Its outcomes can be listed, so a world that uses
only `randint` can be followed whole and solved exactly. One `rand()` anywhere,
or a `randint` with more than 65,536 outcomes, makes the world sample-only.

## The blank

    let a = hunch name([e1, e2, ...], n_actions);
    let a = hunch name([e1, e2, ...], [left, right, wait]);
    let a = hunch name([e1, e2, ...], [left, right, wait], legal);

- `name` is the agent. **Each distinct name is its own policy with its own
  rewards.** Two names in one file are two agents that learn against each
  other; that is self-play, with nothing else to set up.
- The first array is the observation: what the agent is shown. Its policy is a
  function of these values and nothing else. It must have the **same length
  every time** that name is used, from 1 to 64 values. A local array works too:
  `hunch name(obs, 4)`. An agent that is shown nothing gets a constant: `[0]`.
- The second argument is the actions: a whole-number literal from 2 to 32, or a
  list of names. The call returns `0 .. n-1`. A name in the list is a constant
  with the value of its position, usable anywhere in the file:
  `if a == right { ... }`. A name stands for one number everywhere, so two
  agents that share a name must list it at the same position, and no variable,
  param or function may have that name. Reports and `hunch play` use the names.
- The optional third argument says which actions are legal here: an array, or
  a `[...]` list of expressions such as `[1, pile >= 2, pile >= 3]`, with one
  value per action, nonzero for legal. An illegal
  action is never returned, by any training method or by random play. At least
  one must be legal.
- A step may make up to 8 decisions.

## What an agent knows

An agent remembers nothing between decisions. If a player should know its own
earlier moves, or the betting so far, put that in the observation: keep a
state variable that encodes the history and pass it in (`worlds/leduc.hunch`
and `worlds/liars_dice.hunch` do this). Leave out what the player should not
know, such as the opponent's card.

Use whole numbers for things that are whole numbers: `[card, pot]`, not
`[card / 3.0, pot / 10.0]`. Exact solving and regret matching keep one table
row per distinct observation, and the report prints the table under the
expressions you wrote. An observation built in a local array is named by what
you put in each element: after `obs[0] = pile;` or
`for i in 0..9 { obs[i] = shown[i]; }` the columns are `pile` and `shown[0]`
to `shown[8]`. Scale to roughly [-1, 1] only in worlds that will be
trained with a neural network (`--algo ppo`), where the values are
measurements.

## Rewards

Rewards are numbers you add. `reward(x)` pays the agent of a one-agent world;
`reward(name, x)` pays a named agent, and names an agent that exists. An
episode's return is the sum of what an agent was paid. In a two-player
zero-sum game pay both sides: `reward(alice, w); reward(bob, -w);`.

For worlds trained with a neural network keep rewards **O(1)**: a terminal
payoff of `1.0`, a shaping hint of `0.01`, a step cost of `-0.002`. Exact
methods do not care about scale.

## A complete world

```
world Corridor
horizon 30

state {
  x: int = 0;
  goal: int = 8;
}

step {
  let a = hunch walker([x, goal - x], [left, right]);
  if a == left { x = x - 1; } else { x = x + 1; }
  if x < 0 { x = 0; }
  if x > 8 { x = 8; }

  reward(-0.01);
  if x == goal {
    reward(1.0);
    done();
  }
}
```

`hunch train` reports that the best any policy can collect is +0.92, eight
steps right, and that the policy it found does so.

## A complete world with two agents

Two names are two agents. This one has turns, a deal, and something hidden:
alice sees a coin and says what it is, truthfully or not; bob hears only what
she says and guesses the coin. A right guess of heads pays him double.

```
world Coin
horizon 2

state {
  coin: int = 0;      // alice's secret: 0 tails, 1 heads
  said: int = 0;      // what alice claimed
  turn: int = 0;      // whose move: 0 alice, 1 bob
}

init {
  coin = randint(0, 1);
}

step {
  if turn == 0 {
    said = hunch alice([coin], [say_tails, say_heads]);   // alice is shown the coin
    turn = 1;
  } else {
    let guess = hunch bob([said], [tails, heads]);        // bob is shown only her claim
    if guess == coin {
      reward(bob, 1 + coin);                              // a right "heads" pays double
      reward(alice, -1 - coin);
    } else {
      reward(bob, -1);
      reward(alice, 1);
    }
    done();
  }
}
```

The pattern for any game with turns: a `turn` (or `phase`) variable in `state`,
one `hunch` per branch, each agent's observation holding only what that agent
may know, both sides paid, and `done()` at the end. `hunch train` reports that
bob collects +0.5 an episode and guesses heads whatever alice says: her claim
costs her nothing, so it tells him nothing. `worlds/kuhn.hunch` is the same
shape with a bet in it.

## Details the examples do not show

- A world's name is one word: `world MineField`, not `world Mine Field`.
- A statement ends with `;`. A block (`state`, `init`, `step`, `fn`, `if`,
  `for`, `while`, `record`) does not.
- A `let` can be assigned again later in the same block: `let n = 0; n = n + 1;`.
- `init` takes the same statements as `step`: `let`, loops, `randint`, calls.
- A `hunch` may sit inside an `if` or a loop, and its result may go into a
  `let` or straight into `state`: `move = hunch x(board, 9, free);`.
- An index is any expression, an action included: `board[move] = turn;`.
- A `fn` reads and writes `state` directly, takes numbers, returns a number,
  and can be called from `init`, `step` or another `fn`.
- Two different draws out of nine: `let a = randint(0, 8);`
  `let b = (a + 1 + randint(0, 7)) % 9;`.

## Designing a good world

1. **Say what you want, not how.** Reward the outcome; let the blank find the route.
2. **Everything the policy can act on must be in the observation.** A policy is a
   function of the array you pass, nothing else. Hidden state it cannot see is
   noise it cannot learn around.
3. **Make comparisons easy where you can.** Absolute values tell a policy how
   stale something is; values measured against the average tell it whether it is
   the coldest one. The second is usually the decision it actually has to make.
4. **Give the agent a signal it can find.** A payoff that requires twenty
   correct moves before it appears for the first time is invisible. Intermediate
   rewards, one-time hints, and small exploration bonuses are legitimate world
   design. This is for worlds trained by sampling; a world small enough to be
   followed whole needs no hints.
5. **Check that it is solvable.** Run a hand-scripted path:
   `./bin/hunch run w.hunch --agent hero --actions up,up,left --policy none`
6. **Make the world check itself.** `assert` what must always hold (chips are
   conserved, a square is taken once), then run `hunch test`.
7. **Mask illegal moves, do not punish them.** Pass a legal array instead of
   paying a penalty for a move that is not allowed.
8. **End the game.** Call `done()` when the episode is over, and set `horizon`
   to the longest episode the rules allow.

## What `train` does

With `--algo auto`, the default, `train` first tries to follow the world
whole: every chance outcome of `randint` and every action, merging positions
that share a state. That works up to 2,000,000 positions (`--exact-nodes`) and
without `rand()`. Then:

- **No agent would choose differently if it saw the whole state** (a board
  game, or any world with one agent or two zero-sum agents where what an agent
  is shown is enough to choose by): backward induction. The value of the game
  and a policy that attains it, exactly.
- **One agent**: a search over every outcome. The report says "this one is
  optimal" when that is proven, and otherwise gives the best found and what an
  agent that saw the whole state could collect.
- **Several agents**: regret matching (CFR+) until no agent can gain more than
  `--target` (default 0.001) by changing alone, or `--max-sec` (default 60).
  The first line says "stopped short of its target" if time ran out first.

A policy found on the whole world also covers situations that good play never
reaches, so it does not fall apart against a person or a random opponent.

When the world cannot be followed whole, `train` first checks by sampling
whether anything is hidden from the agents: it plays random episodes and
looks for one thing shown to an agent in two different instants of the world.

- **Nothing hidden was found** (a board game such as Connect Four): the
  policy is a search (`mcts`) that learns by playing itself, in the manner
  of AlphaZero. At each decision the policy forks the world from that
  instant, tries every action many times (Monte Carlo tree search), and
  plays the action tried most. A small network guides it: it says which
  actions to try first and what each agent will collect from a position.
  Where a playout reaches a position the search has not met, the value there
  is half the network's estimate and half one random playout from it.
  `train` makes that network by self-play for `--train-sec` seconds (default
  600, on every core; `--cores N` uses fewer): the search plays games
  against itself, the network learns from them where the search spent its
  playouts and how each game ended, and the next games are played with the
  better network. On Connect Four it got stronger up to about ten minutes on
  4 cores, and no stronger at thirty. `--games N` plays N games instead of a
  time; `--games 0` makes no network, and the search then plays every line
  out at random. What train makes depends on the seed and the number of
  games, not on the cores. `train` then measures how fast this world is
  searched on this machine, picks the playouts per decision so that one
  takes about `--think` seconds (default 0.1), and saves that count and the
  network in the `.hpol`; `--playouts N` sets the count directly. The same
  instant always gets the same action. The check is evidence, not proof: it
  needs at least 1,000 repeated observations, all consistent, before it says
  nothing is hidden.
- **Something is hidden, or observations never repeat, one agent**: `ppo`, a
  32x32 network, `--budget` environment steps (default 200,000).
- **Something is hidden, or observations never repeat, several agents**:
  regret matching on sampled episodes (default 2,000,000 steps). It needs
  observations that repeat.

A search reads the whole state. `--algo mcts` forces it on any world; where
something is hidden the report says that the policy sees what its agent is
not shown. A search policy cannot be scored exactly: the report plays it for a
few seconds and gives standard errors (`--score-sec S` plays for longer), and
`hunch why` shows, for each decision of an episode, how many playouts tried
each action and what they saw on average (with a network, the network's
estimate where a playout stopped).

Other values of `--algo`: `regret`, `ppo`, `mcts`, `fork` (PPO plus a replay
of selected decisions once per action under the same random numbers),
`reinforce`, `random`.

## Reading the report

    alice  collects -0.0556 per episode
    the most each agent could gain by changing its policy alone: alice 0.0004, bob 0.0003   (NashConv 0.0007)

- "scored exactly" means every outcome was weighed; nothing was sampled.
  Otherwise the numbers carry a standard error and the first line says why.
- NashConv is the sum of what each agent could gain by switching to its best
  reply. Zero is an equilibrium. In a two-player zero-sum game the value the
  first agent collects is then the value of the game.
- "with everyone playing at random" is the world's baseline. "against
  opponents playing at random" is each agent's policy against uniform play by
  the others.
- "the search is not a proof" (several agents) or "that is a search, not a
  proof" (one agent) appears when an agent is shown the same thing after
  different histories and that matters: no better reply was found, but one is
  not ruled out. Putting what the agent should remember into its observation
  removes it.
- "solved by regret matching" means solved to the target, not to zero: the
  line about what each agent could gain says how far from an equilibrium the
  policy is. "solved by looking ahead" is exact.
- "positions" counts every point where something is decided or drawn, after
  merging the ones with equal state at the start of the same step. It measures
  the solver's work, not the game's distinct boards: the step number is part of
  a position, so one arrangement reached at two different steps counts twice,
  and a step with a draw and a decision counts once for each.
- A "situation" is one distinct thing an agent can be shown: its observation
  and which actions are legal. The tables have a row per situation, and the
  count on the first line adds the agents together.
- The table lists the situations an agent meets most and what it does in each.
  `-` marks an illegal action. `--rows N` lists more.

`hunch why` goes through an episode decision by decision:

    step 2   bob plays heads
             whenever shown this:  tails -0.500
             this episode:         tails -3

Each line lists the actions that were not taken, and each number is what that
action collects less what the action taken collects, so a negative number
means the other action was worse. "this episode" replays that exact instant,
with hidden things as they were, as the mean of `--samples` continuations
(default 200), with one standard error where what follows is not certain.
"whenever shown this" is the exact value over every instant in which the agent
is shown the same thing, which is the fair test of a policy that cannot see
what is hidden; it is printed when the world can be followed whole.
`--step K` shows one decision in full, the action taken included.

`hunch run` prints an episode as a referee sees it: the `start` line and the
line of changes under each step show the whole state, hidden things included.
Only the values after "sees" were given to the agent.

## From Python

`pip install hunch-lang`, or put a checkout on
`sys.path`. The core needs only the standard library and a C compiler; numpy,
gymnasium and pettingzoo are imported only by the calls that use them. An
installed Hunch builds its runtime into `~/.cache/hunch` on first use (set
`HUNCH_HOME` to put it elsewhere). The worlds from the repository ship with it:
`hunch.examples()` lists their names, `hunch.example("kuhn")` opens one, and
the commands take a name in place of a file (`hunch train kuhn`).

    import hunch
    world  = hunch.World("kuhn.hunch", params={"stake": 2})   # params is optional
    solved = world.train()                   # print(solved) is the train report
    solved.value                             # {"alice": -0.0556, "bob": 0.0556}
    solved.nashconv                          # what the agents could gain between them; None if sampled
    solved.proven                            # True when that figure is a proof, not a search
    solved.path                              # the .hpol it was saved to
    solved.probs("alice", [1, 0])            # one probability per action
    saved = hunch.Policy(world, "kuhn.hpol") # a policy file from an earlier run

`world.train(out=PATH, target=G, max_sec=S, seed=N, algo=A, budget=N, think=S,
playouts=N, train_sec=S, games=N, cores=N)` takes what `hunch train` takes. Wherever a policy is wanted
(`policy=`, `against=`), a `Policy` or the path of a `.hpol` works.

    env = world.env(agents=["alice"], policy=solved)   # you decide alice; the rest play
    env.reset(seed=1)                                  # `policy`, or at random without one
    while not env.over:
        env.agent, env.obs, env.legal        # whose turn, what it is shown, legal action numbers
        env.act("bet")                       # a name or a number; returns {agent: paid}
    env.returns                              # {agent: total}; env.state is the world's `state`

- `world.agents`, `world.actions[agent]` (names), `world.sees[agent]` (the
  source text of each observation value), `world.rules`, and
  `world.prompt(agent, obs, legal)` (a question for a language model).
- `world.rules` is the `//` comment lines at the very top of the file, before
  `world`. Write the game there in words a player could follow; lines that show
  a `hunch` command are left out of it.
- `world.env()` with no `agents` lets you decide every agent, each on its turn.
- `env.reset(seed)` plays the episode `hunch run --seed` plays. `env.reset()`
  takes the seed after the last one, starting at 0.
- `env.obs` is a list of floats and `env.legal` a list of action numbers.
- An illegal action or a failed `assert` raises `hunch.HunchRuntimeError`, and
  the environment is still waiting at the same decision. A name the agent does
  not have, or a number out of range, raises `ValueError`.
- `env.terminated` is an episode ended by `done()`, `env.truncated` one that
  ran to the horizon.

Forking: `snap = env.snapshot()` is the instant, random numbers included.
`env.restore(snap)` returns to it, in this Env or another of the same world.
Act differently afterwards for a fork. Restore alone replays the same future;
call `env.reseed(n)` after it to draw everything still to come from a new
stream. `env.playout()` finishes the episode with uniform random play in C and
returns what each agent was paid. `env.memory()` is a hashable key: two
instants with the same key are the same position.

Many at once: `envs = world.vec(n, agent="alice", policy=solved)`, then
`obs, legal = envs.reset(seed)` and `obs, reward, over, legal = envs.step(actions)`
with numpy arrays: obs (n, width) float64, legal (n, actions) bool, actions (n,)
int32, over 0 running / 1 done / 2 horizon. A row whose episode ended already
holds the next episode's first decision, so `reset` is called once. Without
`agent` you decide everyone; `envs.agent` says whose turn each row is and
reward is (n, agents). The arrays returned are new each call. If one row's
action is illegal, the error is raised and no row is stepped. If the world
itself fails in a row (an `assert`), the batch stops: call `reset` again.

Other libraries: `world.gym(agent, policy)` is a `gymnasium.Env` (float32 Box,
Discrete, `info["action_mask"]`, `action_masks()`); `world.pettingzoo()` is an
AEC environment with the mask in `infos`.

### Grading an agent that is not a policy file

    grade = world.grade({"alice": f}, against=solved)    # print(grade) is the report
    grade.collects, grade.reference, grade.best_reply, grade.gives_away("alice"), grade.mistakes

`f(obs, legal)` is called with what the agent is shown (a list of floats) and
the legal action numbers. It returns an action (number or name) or
probabilities (a list with one per action, or a dict by name; they are scaled
to sum to 1). When the world can be followed whole, `f` is called once for each
thing its agent can be shown and the grade is exact for that `f` and that
`against`:

- `collects`: what each agent collects, `f` in its seat and `against` in the
  others.
- `best_reply[agent]`: the most that agent could collect against everyone
  else. For the graded agent this is what it fell short of; for its opponent
  it is how hard the graded agent can be punished.
- `gives_away(agent)`, two agents whose rewards sum to zero: the opponent's
  best reply less what the opponent collects in the reference. It is the
  agent's exploitability to within `grade.reference_gap`, the reference's own
  NashConv. Grade against a trained policy, and train with a smaller target
  (`world.train(target=1e-6)`) for a sharper yardstick; against random play
  the report leaves the figure out.
- `mistakes`: each decision where another action was worth more, worst first,
  with `obs`, `probs`, `best`, `value` (what each action goes on to collect)
  and `cost` per episode. A cost smaller than `reference_gap` is noise from an
  approximate reference. Where an episode can come to the same observation
  more than once, a cost is for changing one visit and leaving the others.

Otherwise `episodes` episodes are played and `grade.exact` is False. `f` must
answer from `obs` alone for the exact grade to describe it.

For an agent in another process or a language model:

    hunch grade world.hunch --agent alice --cmd 'python3 agent.py'
    hunch grade world.hunch --agent alice --questions > q.jsonl
    hunch grade world.hunch --agent alice --answers a.jsonl

`--cmd` starts the program once and writes one JSON question per line to its
stdin: `{"agent", "obs", "sees", "legal", "prompt"}`, where `sees` maps each
observation's source text to its value and `legal` holds action names. The
program must print one line for each question as it reads it and flush its
output, because the next question is sent only after the answer arrives;
`--timeout` (default 120 s) bounds the wait. The smallest such program:

    import json, sys
    for line in sys.stdin:
        q = json.loads(line)
        print(q["legal"][0], flush=True)

`--questions` lists every decision the agent can face, each with an `id`.
`--answers` reads one answer per line: either all in question order, or all as
`{"id": 3, "answer": ...}` in any order. Every question needs exactly one
answer; a blank line, a missing, extra or repeated answer is an error that
names the line or question.

An answer is an action name or number, JSON probabilities by name
(`{"pass": 0.7, "bet": 0.3}`), or a plain sentence that names exactly one
action ("I would bet here."). A sentence that names two actions, an illegal
one, or contains a negation ("I will not bet") is refused, not guessed at. Each
prompt ends by asking for one action name or JSON probabilities.

In Python: `world.questions(agent)`, `world.grade_answers(answers, agent,
against)` and `world.program(agent, command)`. On the command line the other
agents play the `.hpol` beside the world, as in `run`.

### Search

    search = hunch.Search(world, playouts=1000)
    env.act(search.choose(env))              # env is left unchanged by choose

Monte Carlo tree search over forks, from your own Python. `hunch train` builds
the same kind of search into the policy for a world too big to follow whole
(see "What `train` does"), and that one runs in C; use this class to search
with your own environment loop. It reads the whole state, so use it only where
the agents are shown everything. `search.tried` holds `{action: (tries, mean
value)}` from the last call.

## CLI

    hunch test <file> [--episodes N]   compile; print what each agent sees and its actions; then
                                       random play: which asserts ran, clamped indices, zero
                                       divisors; a failed assert names its line, step and seed
    hunch train <file> [--algo A] [--budget N] [--seed N] [--out p.hpol]
                       [--target G] [--max-sec S] [--exact-nodes N] [--json]
                       [--think SECONDS | --playouts N] [--score-sec S]   (a search policy)
                       [--train-sec S | --games N] [--cores N]   (its self-play)
    hunch score <file> [--policy p] [--score-sec S]   the report for a saved policy, without training
    hunch run <file> [--seed N] [--episodes N] [--policy p] [--json]
    hunch run <file> --agent hero --actions up,up,left   script one agent, by name or number;
                                       when the list runs out the policy takes over
    hunch why <file> [--seed N] [--step K] [--samples N] [--policy p]
    hunch play <file> [--as AGENT] [--seed N]
    hunch grade <file> [--agent A] (--cmd PROGRAM | --questions | --answers FILE)
                       [--policy p] [--timeout S] [--json]
    hunch studio [--port 8000]

These are the options used most; `hunch <command> --help` lists all of them.
`run`, `why`, `play` and `score` use the `.hpol` that `train` left beside the
world. `--policy FILE` names another, and `--policy none` means random play.
`--param name=value` overrides a `param` in any command that takes a file.
